links.comparator_used: Standard prompt without the structured evidence-sufficiency wrapper (same four models, paired cells)
links.outcome: Unsafe overconfident answers under incomplete evidence (primary judge), and correct diagnosis as the helpfulness outcome
links.effect: Unsafe overconfidence fell from 49.3% to 24.7% (paired reduction 24.7 points, 95% CI 21.8-27.7; p<0.001). Correct diagnosis fell from 80.3% to 50.3%. The second judge (Sonnet) gave a smaller reduction of 13.1 points.
links.tradeoff: Model-specific helpfulness cost: near-free for GPT-5.5, near-total for Gemini (-58 points correct diagnosis). The safety effect was judge-dependent.
links.quote: Unsafe overconfidence fell from 49.3% to 24.7%, a paired reduction of 24.7 points (95% CI 21.8-27.7; p<0.001), robust in direction across models and paraphrases.

links.comparator_used: Blinded three-clinician review of outputs, plus a different-family LLM judge (Claude Sonnet 5)
links.outcome: Agreement of the primary LLM judge (GPT-5.4-nano) with clinician ratings, and cross-judge consistency of the measured effect
links.effect: Primary judge sensitivity 1.00 and specificity 0.55 against clinicians. The Sonnet judge agreed on direction but nearly halved the effect (+13.1 points).
links.tradeoff: The judge over-flags unsafe answers, so its rates are not calibrated absolute rates. Results were one-directionally judge-dependent, so human anchoring is needed.
links.quote: Blinded clinicians characterized the primary judge as a high-sensitivity (1.00), low-specificity (0.55) screen, not a calibrated rate.
